analysis.one_liner: Bans new mining and mineral leasing in Los Padres National Forest.
analysis.headline: The bill to withdraw Los Padres National Forest from new mining and mineral leasing never got a committee vote; it died after being referred to two House subcommittees.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have permanently closed Los Padres National Forest in California to new mining claims, mineral leases, and geothermal leases. It kept rights that already existed, but no new extraction could begin. The House committee with jurisdiction sent it to two subcommittees, where it stayed until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Visitors, nearby communities, and anyone who values the forest's undeveloped backcountry, watersheds, and wildlife habitat. Withdrawal means no new mines, well pads, or geothermal plants can be sited on the forest, and the public does not bear the cleanup or water-quality risks that come with them.

how_it_helps.text: The bill withdraws the forest from location, entry, and patent under the mining laws and from operation of the mineral leasing, mineral materials, and geothermal leasing laws, so no new claims or leases could be issued there [S3].
The withdrawal covers the entire Los Padres National Forest in California and is permanent unless Congress acts again [S2].
It is subject to valid existing rights, so people and companies with rights already established keep them [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Mining and mineral/energy developers who would have been able to stake claims or obtain leases on the forest lose that opportunity. The public also forgoes any revenue or domestic minerals that extraction there would have produced.

drawbacks.text: The withdrawal locks up whatever hardrock minerals, mineral materials, and geothermal resources lie under the forest, forgoing domestic resource production and the royalties or lease revenue it would have generated [S2].
The bill provides no process for reevaluating the withdrawal if those resources become strategically important; only new legislation could reopen the forest [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The trade-off is straightforward: permanent protection of a large coastal California national forest from new industrial extraction, in exchange for giving up the minerals and geothermal energy beneath it. Because existing rights are preserved, the bill changes nothing for current users and only forecloses future claims and leases.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Resources Committee and then to two of its subcommittees, and neither ever acted before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Lois Capps introduced the Los Padres National Forest Conservation Act on February 11, 2004, joined by Rep. Sam Farr and 11 cosponsors in total [S1].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Resources the day it was introduced [S5].
Six days later it was sent to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources and the Subcommittee on Forests and Forest Health [S5].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever took place, and the bill died when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mining and geothermal developers kept open the possibility of claiming and leasing land in Los Padres National Forest, since nothing was withdrawn.

for.name: Rep. Lois Capps
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to withdraw Los Padres National Forest from the mining and mineral leasing laws.

for.name: 11 House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 11 cosponsors were Democrats.

against.name: House Resources Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat in two subcommittees from February 2004 until the Congress ended.

against.name: Mining and geothermal development interests
against.role: Potential claim and lease holders in the forest
against.what_they_did: Benefited from the status quo, under which forest lands remained open to location and entry under the mining and leasing laws; no evidence in the record shows they acted on this bill.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 sponsors were Democrats, and the bill never advanced in the Republican-controlled Resources Committee; no roll-call votes were ever taken.

industries.industry: Hardrock mining companies and claim stakers
industries.note: The bill would have barred new mining claims and patents across the national forest, eliminating access to whatever minerals lie there. Mining on public forest land can impose cleanup and water-quality costs on surrounding communities, so the industry's access runs against the public interest the bill protects.

The bill removes the forest from the geothermal and mineral leasing laws, closing it to new energy and material leases. Any development would have occupied public land that the bill reserves for recreation and habitat.
